profile.name: Md Motasim Billa
profile.statusHtml: MS student in Information Science at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock.
bio: I am a master’s student in Information Science at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock. My studies are about something simple and important: how knowledge is made, organized, and shared — how what one person learns finds its way to others. I also care about fairness in science. The people who do the work should get the credit they deserve, and people should be able to trust what they read.

My story began in Dhaka, Bangladesh, among books and libraries. Later, I worked as a journalist. Every day I asked questions, and I learned to check what is true before I wrote it down. Then came a fellowship year in America, and it opened a whole new world to me. Step by step, that path brought me to information science, and to Arkansas.

I love travelling and seeing new places. I love exploring different fields of study, and new technology always makes me curious. I enjoy reading, and I enjoy a good debate. My road has taken me through libraries, newsrooms, and classrooms in two countries — and I am still curious about where it leads next.

publications.heading: Publications
publications.intro: The center of this site — peer-reviewed and forthcoming work, grouped by year, newest first. My name appears in bold in each author list.

entries.title: The Invisible Infrastructure of Biomedical Research: An Exploratory Analysis of Software Mentions and Sentence-Level Citation Marking
entries.note: Modern biomedical papers run on software that is usually mentioned in passing rather than cited. This study maps those software mentions across the literature and examines sentence-level citation marking — where in a paper credit is given, and what that placement says about how scholarly credit actually flows.

entries.title: Livelock in the Agent Harness: Delegation-Induced Liveness Failure in LLM Systems
entries.authorsHtml: M. Hasan, A. Khan, H. Rashid, M. M. Billa, S. Islam, and M. Milanova · Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Trust, Privacy and Security in Intelligent Systems and Applications (TPS) · 2026 · Application Track
entries.note: Studies livelock in LLM agent harnesses — systems where agents keep delegating work to one another and nothing ever finishes — and names and characterizes this delegation-induced liveness failure. To appear; one of 16 papers accepted from 146 submissions.

entries.title: A Position-Based Citation-Credit Model for Multi-Authored Publications
entries.authorsHtml: M. M. Billa · University of Arkansas at Little Rock · Advisor: Daniel Berleant, Ph.D.
entries.note: A citation is a single unit of credit, but a paper can have two authors or two hundred — and where a name sits in the byline carries information flat counting throws away. This thesis develops a position-sensitive model for allocating that credit among co-authors, and tests how different attribution choices change researcher-level bibliometric assessment.

newspaper.heading: My newspaper articles
newspaper.intro: My bylined work for the press — fact-checks and investigations for The Dissent, and my earlier newspaper reporting from Dhaka, kept as clippings.
introParagraphsHtml: Before graduate school I reported from Dhaka University for the Bengali daily Shomoyer Alo (byline: Motasim Billa Naim), covering the campus in 2019 — admission reform, student movements, and the small stories in between. From 2023 to 2024 I was a data journalist at Bangladesh Post in Dhaka, where I wrote more than 200 data-informed and analytical articles: turning datasets, budgets, and official statistics into evidence-based, public-interest reporting that readers could check for themselves. That newsroom training — ask what the numbers actually say, and show your working — is the same instinct I now bring to scientometrics.

Like most newspaper stories, the printed pieces below ran in two parts: a first part under the headline, and the rest continued — “jumped” — to an inside page. Each card below shows only the titled first part, complete and uncropped. Click a clipping to read it enlarged — and where the continuation page survives among my scans, it appears there, after the first part, exactly as a reader of the paper would have turned to it. Where no continuation page is among my scans, the enlarged view says so rather than filling the gap.
newspaper.factCheckIntro: Fact-checks and digital investigations I wrote for The Dissent, an independent Bangladeshi fact-checking outlet — each one opens the full story on thedissent.news.

factChecks.title: Eurasia Review’s Claim about UN Dhaka Office: What’s behind it?
factChecks.summary: The claim that Bangladesh rejected the UN’s nominee for Resident Coordinator in Dhaka was false — neither the government nor the UN had made any decision — and the op-ed’s author and outlet do not hold up to scrutiny.
factChecks.imageAlt: Cover image for the Eurasia Review investigation: the Eurasia Review logo beside a portrait of the op-ed’s author

factChecks.title: Dozens of false claims traced to India as Bangladesh prepares for vote
factChecks.summary: In the 60 days after the election schedule was announced, 39 widely circulated false or misleading claims were traced to India — nine through Indian news outlets and thirty through India-run social media accounts.
factChecks.imageAlt: Cover image for the India disinformation report: a silhouetted head filled with the Indian flag over a digital circuit pattern

factChecks.title: “Which One Do You Like?”: Girl Students Sexualised in Madrasa Teachers’ TikTok Videos
factChecks.summary: Madrasa teachers filmed their young students and posted the videos to TikTok with sexualised captions inviting viewers to pick which child they liked — without any parent’s permission.
factChecks.imageAlt: Cover image for the madrasa TikTok investigation: three TikTok screenshots of madrasa students, their faces obscured, with suggestive Bengali captions

factChecks.title: Network Uses Fake Credentials and Deepfake Videos to Market ‘Sexual Disease’ Drugs
factChecks.summary: A network of 50 Facebook pages used deepfake videos of popular Islamic speaker Mizanur Rahman Azhari, fake licences and staged reviews to run 590 ads selling unauthorised sexual-health drugs.
factChecks.imageAlt: Cover image for the deepfake-drugs investigation: screenshots of fake Facebook ads using Mizanur Rahman Azhari’s image to sell Ginseng and Urocin products

factChecks.title: Awami League amplifies misinformation citing suspicious website as US media
factChecks.summary: The ‘US media outlet’ cited for the claim that Washington spent $320 million to remove the Hasina government is no established American news organisation at all — it is run largely from Bangladesh, and the claim itself has no evidence behind it.
factChecks.imageAlt: Cover image for the CSB News USA verification: screenshots of Awami League-linked pages sharing the ‘Paper Trail’ report alongside a portrait of Sheikh Hasina

chronicles.heading: Chronicles
chronicles.intro: The chapters behind the CV — the fellowship year and the student leadership. The facts and dates live on the CV page; these are the experiences I would rather tell properly.

stories.tabTitle: The CCI Year — Md Motasim Billa
stories.title: The CCI year — the best experience of my life
stories.introHtml: A U.S. Department of State fellowship took me to Northern Virginia Community College for a year of study, service, and exchange. I still call it, without hesitation, one of the best experiences of my life.
stories.pageMeta: 2021 – 2022 · Virginia, USA · U.S. Department of State CCI Program
paragraphsHtml: In 2021 I was selected for the Community College Initiative (CCI) Program, a U.S. Department of State fellowship that brings participants from around the world to spend an academic year at an American community college. I still call it, without hesitation, one of the best experiences of my life. My placement was Northern Virginia Community College, where I studied Business Management and Leadership Development, completed an Associate’s degree (GPA 3.42/4.00), and earned a place on the Dean’s Honor List in Spring 2022.

But the degree was only part of what CCI is designed to give. The program deliberately builds a year out of more than coursework — internships, community service, and cultural exchange are woven through it — and it was those parts that stayed with me most. I volunteered as a Book Buddy with Alexandria City Public Schools, sitting with young readers one-to-one each week and watching hesitant kids turn into confident ones. I lived the ordinary rhythms of Northern Virginia: classes, work, service, and the small daily negotiations of a new country. For a student from Bangladesh, it was a full year of seeing how another society organizes its schools, its libraries, and its public life — from the inside.

That year changed the direction of mine. It reshaped how I think about education and public institutions, gave me friends and mentors across the world, and planted the idea that I would come back to the United States for graduate study. When I arrived at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock for my MS in Information Science, I was, in a real sense, continuing a journey that CCI started.

stories.title: Leading BYI — the Bangladesh Youth Initiative
stories.introHtml: Before the fellowship came a lesson in leading at home: a year as president of the Bangladesh Youth Initiative’s Dhaka University unit — holding an organization together, and answering for the result.
paragraphsHtml: Before the fellowship came a lesson in leading at home. At the University of Dhaka I served as president of the university unit of the Bangladesh Youth Initiative (BYI) in 2020–21 — a student community built around young people taking responsibility for something larger than their own degrees. The presidency was my first real experience of holding an organization together: setting a direction, persuading busy students to give their time to it, and answering for the result when plans met reality.

It taught me things no classroom had. Leadership, I learned, is mostly listening carefully and following through — doing the unglamorous work between meetings that makes the visible work possible. In the same season I coordinated Surjasen Bitarka Dhara, the debating circle of Surjasen Hall (2020), which sharpened the other half of the skill: building an argument, defending it in public, and losing one gracefully. Those Dhaka years — organizing, debating, reporting for the campus paper — are the foundation everything since has been built on.
